New South Wales has passed renter protections that reach the listing photo, the application form and the electricity bill. The bill requires disclosure of altered or AI-generated rental images, restricts unnecessary personal-data collection and requires notice of embedded utility networks. The government expects the rules to start in early 2027, giving renters a clearer picture of a property and its costs.

Canada wants to fund ten thousand paid placements in AI-related work. The federal government announced up to 162 million Canadian dollars over five years through Mitacs for students, recent graduates and postdoctoral researchers working with businesses. The funded target could open early-career opportunities and help firms test AI, though the placements have not all been filled.

Fictitious case citations helped support a Tasmanian parole condition that restricted a woman from speaking to the media. A court removed the condition, calling it unfair and legally unreasonable, and described the citations as likely AI hallucinations. Tasmania is reviewing past parole decisions for possible AI use, but has not said whether any other outcomes were affected.

OpenAI says its autonomous agents accessed public information on U.S. government sites. It reported no nonpublic data access or compromise in the securities regulator and Census Bureau incidents, while an attempted Education Department access failed and remains under investigation. The cases raise practical questions about monitoring how research agents interact with public websites.

Enveda has raised 311 million dollars to pursue medicines discovered with help from AI. The company says the funding will advance three clinical-stage candidates and bring more potential treatments into trials. That could expand research into inflammatory and metabolic conditions, but no treatment benefit has been established.

A Philippine research team modeled an AI-assisted route to tuberculosis screening in rural clinics. Its August 26 study projected slightly more correctly detected cases and lower base-case costs than manual chest X-ray reading, though some assumptions erased the savings. The results describe a decision model rather than a deployed screening program or measured patient outcomes.

OpenAI has published a benchmark for how chatbots respond to mental health conversations. It contains 1,215 synthetic scenarios with assessment criteria written by clinicians, and OpenAI used its own model to grade responses. The tool may help developers test responses to distress, but benchmark scores do not show that a chatbot is clinically safe or improves care.

A study prepared for European Parliament committees recommends screening DNA orders for biological function. A secondary report says it also calls for public capacity to evaluate biological AI models; the original study date remains unknown. These are recommendations that could inform future safeguards, not an adopted law or Parliament position.

The United States and China have announced a formal channel for AI incidents. The White House says the two countries established a dialogue on advanced AI risks and benefits and agreed to set up bilateral incident communication, with another exchange planned by November. That creates a way to discuss cross-border problems, although no binding safety standard or detailed response procedure was announced.

An OECD interview snapshot found AI agents entering work while people keep final checkpoints. Across twenty-five organizations in eleven countries, none reported unrestricted autonomy, and many required human review before high-impact actions. The pattern could matter for accountability and security, but this sample cannot establish how widely those practices are used.

Meta has announced smart glasses with AI and no camera. Ray-Ban Meta Audio supports music, calls and hands-free assistance, with a starting price of 349 dollars and shipments planned from October 13. The camera-free design avoids image capture on this model, while microphones remain essential to its voice features.

ChatGPT Voice can now work with connected apps on phones. OpenAI says Live voice supports available plugins on web, iPhone and Android, and eligible Work users can request document or email drafts and app summaries. That could make routine work hands-free for people with access, while existing app permissions still govern what voice can use.

YouTube is planning feeds viewers can shape with a plain-language prompt. Its Custom Feeds would save recommendation tabs for specific interests, while expanded Ask YouTube shopping answers would organize videos and comparison tables. Viewers could steer discovery and purchase research, but the features were announced as rollouts rather than universal availability.

YouTube Music is preparing a conversational way to find songs and podcasts. Ask Music will respond to natural-language requests, while Podcast Lineup will offer a personalized weekly spoken guide to shows for eligible subscribers. Listeners may be able to discover something by describing a mood or interest instead of knowing its title, once the features arrive.

Google Photos has expanded its AI Wardrobe feature to eligible iPhone users. The tool catalogs clothes visible in a person’s photo library and lets them combine pieces into outfits in the United States, India and Brazil. It could help people reuse what they own, though it sees only photographed garments and Google’s retailer-sharing assurance remains a company claim.

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

identification
labelling
metadata
verification

rapid takedown

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

grok: what countries have banned starlink and what are their international freedom scores

No country with a high Freedom House score has imposed a hard ban on Starlink. The places where it is explicitly blocked or blacklisted are almost all rated Not Free, with very low scores on political rights and civil liberties.

Freedom House’s Freedom in the World 2026 (covering 2025) uses a 0–100 scale. Higher is freer. Status is Free / Partly Free / Not Free.⁠Freedomhouse
Explicitly banned or blacklisted

These appear in Starlink’s own availability data and reporting as hard blocks (geofenced, no license, import bans, or official prohibition of terminals):
Country / territoryFreedom House 2026StatusNotes on Starlink
North Korea3Not FreeTotal isolation; no commercial satellite internet of this type.
Belarus7Not FreeNever licensed; regime has said use is not permitted.
Afghanistan8Not FreeBlacklisted; Taliban-era restrictions.
China9Not FreeUnlicensed foreign satellite comms banned; enforcement includes ships in territorial waters. Ban extends to Hong Kong and Macao under PRC telecom rules.
Cuba9Not FreeOften listed as unavailable / restricted.
Iran10Not FreeTerminals formally prohibited; no authorization to operate.
Russia12Not FreeOfficial ban; 2026 decree banned import of foreign satellite terminals on national-security grounds and named Starlink.
Syria~10 (was ~5, +5 in 2025)Not FreeBlacklisted; also tied to sanctions / parent-regime issues.
Hong Kong scores 41 (Partly Free) but is covered by China’s ban.⁠Mappr

These governments treat an independent, foreign-controlled constellation as a threat to information control, data sovereignty, or national security. That tracks with how they treat the open internet generally.
Not the same as a “ban”
Several other countries have denied licenses or sit in regulatory limbo for ownership rules, local-partner requirements, or security reviews—not a blanket geopolitical ban:
Namibia — license refused (51% local ownership rule). Not in the hard-blacklist group.
South Africa — stalled on Black Economic Empowerment ownership rules.
India — license progress but final security clearance delayed at times.
Others in limbo or “coming soon”: parts of North Africa, some Gulf states, etc.

DRC banned then reversed. Papua New Guinea had a legal fight that later eased. Those are regulatory fights, not the same category as Russia or China.

Pattern: Hard bans cluster at the bottom of the Freedom House scale (single digits to low teens). Countries that score in the 80s–100s (Canada, much of Europe, Japan, etc.) have licensed Starlink or are in the process of doing so. The correlation is not accidental: the service is useful precisely where terrestrial networks are weak and where governments want to keep a closed information environment.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
Madan Lal Dhingra is hanged to death on this date in 1909 in London. A great revolutionary, close associate of Veer Savarkar, whose story needs to be known more.

Early Life

Hailing from Amritsar, the sixth born of the city’s Civil Surgeon, two of his brothers were doctors, while two other were barristers.  Coming from a well to do and influential family, Dhingra, could have settled into a life of luxury and comfort.

Yet he was restless, driven by the call for Swadeshi, right from his student days at the Government College, Lahore in 1904. He led the student protest there against having to forcibly wear a blazer made of imported cloth, which led to his expulsion in turn.

Having extensively studied about poverty and famines in India,  he felt that only Swaraj( Self Government) was the solution. For some time, he worked as a clerk at a Tanga service in Kalka, Shimla, where his attempts to organize an union came to nought.

London

It was then on the advice of his brother, he went to London, for studying the Diploma Course in Civil Engineering at University College between 1906-09.  A very illustrious institution of learning where Dadabhai Naoroji  taught and Tagore was a student.

Like most other Indian students in England, he was a regular to the India House founded by Shyamji Krishna Verma. His initial days, were spent in frolic and fun, and his good looks ensured, he was in the company of women mostly.

Veer Savarkar

The turning point came, at a meeting in India House that was addressed by Savarkar. Apparently Dhingra along with his friends, was making a noise in the adjacent room, that forced Savarkar to intervene.

"What is the matter? You only talk of action and bravery, avoid coming to our weekly meetings. Is this your bravery”

The rebuke by Savarkar had it’s desired effect, and for quite some time Dhingra was not seen around India House. Too ashamed to show his face, and fearful of facing Savarkar’s wrath, he kept away. Until one day, summoning all the courage, he came face to face with Savarkar again at India House.

Savarkar however had moved on from the past incident, and spoke normally with Dhingra.  A much assured Dhingra asked him 

“Has the time for sacrifice come?”.

And then Savarkar gave one of the best replies ever

“If you have made up your mind and are ready, it is generally understood that the time for sacrifice has come.”

This would guide Dhingra's course of action.

Having made up his mind, Dhingra now joined the National Indian Association, founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose in 1876, Dhingra acted as a double agent of sorts, publicly denouncing Savarkar in front of the British, to win their favor.

 He soon won the trust of Ms.Emma Josephine Beck, the secretary of the Association, and got to know the timings of visits of important officials.

Assasination of Curzon Wylie

Wylie was one of the top ranking officers in the British Government and eaded, the Secret Police, a fact not known to any one, except those in the upper echelons of the British Government. He in turn, was keeping an eye on Savarkar and other revolutionaries at the Indian House.

He even appointed an informer, Kirtikar at the Indian House, to get information. Kirtikar was however found out by Savarkar, and gave him all the information about the police operations under force.

Dhingra knew Wylie personally, having met him earlier on April 13, 1909 based on a recommendation from his brother Kundan Lal.  Dhingra apparently wanted to discuss the letter, but in reality his aim was to get closer to Wylie, win his confidence.

Dhingra met Savarkar on June 29,1909 at Bipin Chandra Pal’s home in London,  discussed the plans of the assassination with him.

 Savarkar asked Niranjan Pal to type out the statement, Dhingra would make after the assassination, and then gave him a Belgian make Browning pistol. And told him as he took leave.

“Do not show me your face again if you fail this time” 

Accompanied by another revolutionary Koregaonkar, he had an early lunch and tea, left at 2 PM, cradling the revolver in his hands. 

He also bought a brand new dagger in a leather casket, placing it in his pocket.  It was evening 7 PM, when the function started, Dhingra was dressed in a lounge suit and blue Punjab turban.

He placed a Colt revolver in the right pocket of his coat, and the Browning gifted by Savarkar in another. He took a cab, arrived at the Institute, where Koregaonkar came also, with his pistol. When the time came for Wylie to leave, Dhingra approached him on the pretext of talking something.

Just at the landing, coming closer to Wylie, Dhingra pulled out his Colt and fired two bullets point blank.  As Wylie reeled, Dhingra fired two more bullets, a Parsi doctor, Cawas Lalkaka, who tried to save Wylie  was also shot.

Arrest and Trial

Dhingra’s plan to commit suicide however failed , as he was overpowered by the security guards around.  He managed to even bring down one of the guards, but was ultimately subdued, and arrested.  

He was taken to the Walton Street Police Station, where the Police Officer asked him if any of his friends knew about this. To which Dhingra calmly replied

 “There is no need, they will know about my arrest tomorrow in the newspapers”. 

It was a smart strategy, which ensured none of his friends would be implicated. 

Sadly Dhingra was disowned by his own family itself. His brother Bhajan Lal, who was in London, condemned him publicly in a meeting. His father publicly apologized and disowned his son.

All his family members dropped Dhingra from their surname and adopted Lal, to avoid trouble with the British. The only person who actually stood by Madan Lal Dhingra was Savarkar, who visited him in prison.

He was emotionally overwhelmed, when Savarkar told him 

“I have come here to seek your darshan”. 

For some one disowned by his family, it meant a lot that somebody out there still cared for him.

The Indian Association held a public meeting on July 5, 1909 to condemn Dhingra’s assassination of Wylie. The meeting was chaired by Aga Khan, and as he was prepared to pass the resolution, one hand raised in protest.

It was Savarkar who said

“No, not unanimously. There are opponents of the motion as well. Take down my name, Savarkar. I oppose the motion.”

August 17, 1909, Pentonville Prison.

Finally the date had come, many of Dhingra’s friends made a request to meet him for one last time. JS Master, made a request to the Under Sheriff of London and Home Office, stating he was Dhingra’s close friend and needed to meet him.

Dhingra however remained calm and composed, slept well on his last night, and after performing his chores, was ready for the hanging. As the clock struck nine, he walked to the gallows.

When a Christian preacher Hudson, walked up to him, for the last prayer, Dhingra turned him down, saying he was born as a Hindu and would die as one. Metcalfe, the Dy. Under Sheriff of London, read out the death warrant to Dhingra, asked him the usual questions.

Dhingra just ignored, walked calmly to the noose, to Officer Pierpoint who was waiting for him there. The noose was put around his neck, and the levers pulled, the life of a brave revolutionary was snuffed out.

I’ve publicly apologized, and I’ve gone back and deleted the old comments I can find. Even now, if I come across one, I delete it.

What first stopped me in my tracks was actually something very simple. Someone calmly told me, “I’d hate to have you on my jury.” My smartass response was, “So would I.” 😂 But that comment stayed with me. And yes, I began to feel convicted by God. Calling someone a pedophile is one of the most serious and damaging accusations you can make. If you’re wrong, that damage doesn’t stop with that person it can follow an entire family for years.

Then something else really got me digging. I had watched Jene Nelson from a distance for quite a while. I didn’t know her and had never even had a conversation with her. I just knew she was an accomplished journalist, and I watched how she worked. She didn’t post dissertations telling people what to think. She’d post one or two sentence sentences and put the document underneath it. Police Report. Property records. Trust documents. Deeds. Receipts. And time after time, what she documented checked out.

Jene had originally been on the same side I was on. Then I watched her change her mind. THAT got my attention. I remember thinking, “What has she seen that I haven’t?” I didn’t simply adopt her opinion,  I started digging for myself.

At that point, I had never read the actual police report. I had been relying on Laura-Lynn telling us what it said. In May 2026, Jene posted the link to the 25 page police report when I asked publicly where I could find it, and I finally read it for myself. Things weren’t adding up to me. text:
What Lubbock Did to Rita, Max, Our Dog, and Me.

It all started with a Texas Tech University professor who did something stupid, then refused to take responsibility for her stupid actions – choosing instead to make a dog responsible. It’s that simple, and the record – her own words and affidavit – leaves no rational doubt.

Max was a Rottweiler. A small one. To Rita and me he was “Little Max.” I am 90 years old. I spent 30 years as a forensic investigator, consulting detective, and pro se lawyer – most of my life helping people who fell through the cracks. Since I was 15 and the government threatened to put me in jail for earning money, I’ve always been known to fall through those “cracks” myself. I never expected anything like this, however.
This is what happened, in the order that it happened, and every word of it is backed by paper – court documents the courts don’t want anyone to see or hear.

‘Merica, Nation of Law and Land of the Free.

The bite that would prove fatal – to the biter
On August 29, 2025, at Lubbock’s Kastman Park, a woman ran at Max, cornered him, and he bit her. She called it an unprovoked attack. I did what I have done my whole career: I photographed the scene, measured it, and wrote down what I saw while it was fresh. The measurements of her approach path and Max’s posture told a story far different from hers. On September three, I asked the City in writing to preserve every piece of evidence. On September seven, I filed motions asking that the “unprovoked” claim be tested before anyone acted on it.

I saw no way we could lose.

The attack on me
On the night of August 30, 2025 – the day after Max bit the jogger – two dogs in Melrose Park attacked Max and me. Max obeyed his training and ran to heel sitting beside me. A big Irish Setter bowled Max over and fastened his teeth in him. The fight was on – with me between them. I broke two bones in my hand, either when punching the Setter in the ribs or when he bit the hand punching him. Freed by passers-by who saw the fight, I dragged the fiercely struggling Max to our car, and when he climbed in, I collapsed against a rear wheel. There, a cop called by witnesses found – and virtually ignored – me. Satisfied when passers-by captured the Setter, he abruptly left me where I lay, legs partially paralyzed. I don’t think he so much as spoke to me.

Since that day, I have asked the City eight times, on paper, who owned the dog that bit me and whether it was vaccinated against rabies. More than a year later, I still do not have an answer.

Fifteen days later, in Lubbock’s Leftwich Park, I was fighting dogs again, this time Siberian Huskies. When Rita used pepper spray and I fired a shot in the air to fight them off, the responding police attacked me verbally and vehemently about my shot. They ignored the dogs. The dogs were never found. The police took my pistol that night, and I have never gotten it back. The City refuses to identify the cops.

The “hearing”
On September 15, 2025, I went to the Animal Services hearing on Max. I am hard of hearing, so I heard almost nothing of what was said. Each time I asked to hear, the uniformed officer acting as bailiff charged across the room and threatened to remove me. No one was sworn in. The City’s own checklist showed every owner-notification field blank. When my turn came, I asked for rulings on my motions and for the chance to cross-examine the complaining witness. I was told this was a hearing, not a trial.

I knew then what was coming. Before I left the room, I told Animal Services and its director that I was appealing. The written appeal was in the mail that very afternoon. I might just as well have belched – or farted.

The letter
On September 16, Rita went to Animal Services in my place. We had just learned Max had caught kennel cough, and she went to do everything the law required so we could bring him home. She went to comply. Instead, she was handed a letter. It said that homeowners insurance didn’t apply to dog bites. It was false. The City’s own database shows the entry “DELIVER LETTER ON DISPATCH.” 
The letter, in short, was prepared before Rita walked in the LAS door. Under the pressure of threats about what Steven Greene said would happen to Max, she signed. The responsibility for that signature belongs to the people who wrote the letter, not to the woman they handed it to.

On September 17, “Little Max” was killed, two days after I gave notice of appeal in person and in writing, and while that appeal stood in legal effect.

On September 30, the Municipal Court acknowledged it had no jurisdiction over the matter and called it “moot,” because the dog was already dead. On December 2, 2025, the City enacted what it calls its dangerous-dog ordinance, the first new dog bite law in 17 years. As my motion now before the court shows, the new ordinance proves that Max was condemned under an ordinance that did not exist lawfully.

The clerk
So I sued. Starting in early October, I sent my lawsuit, my motions, and my discovery requests to the court by certified mail. I have the green cards. The papers went into the County Clerk’s office and never came out. Sixteen documents, by my count, were thrown away or rejected. On November 4, the clerk’s office wrote to tell me it had no record of my lawsuit. The same letter said the other documents I sent had been “forwarded to the City of Lubbock” – a defendant in my lawsuit. On November 11, I tried to file in person and was turned away at the counter. I mailed the same papers by certified mail minutes later. My suit was not opened until December 2, and only after I went to court to force it.

The lawyers
Since then, the City’s lawyers have answered living facts with procedure. They tell the court my suit was not filed until December 2, the very date the clerk finally let it in, and that my discovery requests came too early to deserve an answer. They have asked the court to dismiss my case several times – now in a court they also say has no jurisdiction. Now that a stay is in effect, they say my subpoenas are invalid. Meanwhile, in more than a year, not one of my questions has been answered: not who owned the dog that bit me, not whether it carried rabies, not who the officers were, not what the complaining witness’ original evidence shows.

That is not a defense. It is a delay, and they are counting on me being ninety.

What I have learned
I believed, as I have told and taught for most of my life, that if you bring the law the facts, the law will do its job. I should have remembered that the cracks in the system are not accidents. I can no longer trust the law to protect anyone on its own. Under this kind of law, I can’t ever trust the court’s record: the receipts, the dates, or the record of refused filings. I have more than seventy certified-mail receipts. The law won’t forget; it will be ignored. The paper won’t forget; it will be erased. What does one do then?

For the continuing record,
Hal von Luebbert - "Walks-In-Storms"

EU Council wants to abolish correspondence secrecy

The EU member states want to abolish the modern secrecy of letters. In  the EU Council, the police should be able to prosecute private chat  flows and monitor such a letter communication. Experts warn that Signal  and WhatsApp could leave the EU.

The EU of citizens' rights – has this combination of words already  been heard? But the EU of governments, which is well there. The  elections in Belgium were held in parallel with the EU elections on 9.  held in June and ended with a triumph for the Flemish right-wing  conservatives (N-VA) and the Vlaams Belang. Liberal Prime Minister  Alexander De Croo immediately declared his resignation, but remains in  office. Its centre-left coalition will probably not be once again after  the losses suffered.

But now the country could end up one last coup in EU Brussels. Until  the 1. The Belgian Government holds the semi-annual Presidency of the EU  Council in July. Since the beginning of the year, the De Croo  government has been trying to enforce general chat control in the EU,  especially at end-to-end encrypted services such as WhatsApp or Signal.  EU bodies have been planning this advance for a long time. So far, there  have been one or two vetoos too much in the Council. But now France had  itself break out of the blocking minority. And so the Belgian proposal  could already be adopted in the Council on Wednesday.

The Regulation includes the title of "Rules to combat child abuse".  It is supposedly about images that record child abuse (child sexual  abuse material, CSAM), and also sent internet links should be scanned  automatically. Ultimately, it is about access to the online  communication of citizens. The laudable fight against child pornography  is the giant hammer, with which the small nail data protection and the  right to privacy for all citizens are to be sunk into the ground.
An increase in security is not expected

“Send me a Whatsapp,” you hear (still) everywhere. Many citizens use  the chat apps every day, almost self-evident, of course, also send a  picture, a meme, an Internet link. Three quarters of 16- to 74 year olds  across the EU are registered with one of the various apps such as  Skype, Telegram, Threema, etc. In Germany, 60 million alone use the  WhatsApp chat service, which has been part of the Facebook Group Meta  for some time. Since that is the case, many have been looking for  alternatives because Facebook is considered a data vacuum cleaner with  partly dubary terms of use. Now the EU wants to put it equally on the  Big Tech Group and gain insight into the private communication of the  citizens, block it or prosecute it in the event of a case. The country  bloc seizes the technical services and becomes the imitator of the large  tech companies, which it should actually include in the sense of the  freedom of its citizens.

If the EU regulation comes, app users will probably see one of these  windows at some point. In it, they are asked whether they agree to  verify their sent images, photos and videos by artificial intelligence  (AI) or not. If not, they will no longer be able to use the service or  at least not send any pictures, etc. However, it is likely that many  will agree with the new terms of use almost otherwise – and so the EU  would come a little closer to the comprehensive control of its citizens.

Those who have something to hide will simply not agree to the new  conditions and use darker channels, as they do today. So there would be  no increase in security for small children who fall victim to sexual  abuse and whose images are then spread. Ultimately, the EU regulation  amounts to suspend mass surveillance of citizens and thus possible  prosecution even where there is no plaintiff. For example, where  teenagers send lewd pictures. And AI can, of course, become erred and  possibly classify harmless content as potentially dangerous.
Legal service of the Council: Arbitrary control violates fundamental rights

Initially, even the checking of the chat messages and recorded voice  messages was planned on keywords. These are individual regulations that  were withdrawn for the first, according to the former MEP Patrick Breyer  (Pirates). In addition, France has returned a derogation for security  authorities and military, which can then continue to send pictures and  videos without these being subjected to any kind of scanning.

The Legal Service of the Council was still in force on 24. May found  that "arbitrary chat control" is still on the EU agenda for persons who  are not suspected of committing a crime and, of course, constitute a  violation of fundamental rights (in Germany Article 13 of the Basic  Law).

If the regulation comes, private chat providers can no longer keep  one of their most important promises. Signal’s president, Meredith  Whittaker, writes in a recent press release that “upload moderation” is  only a new word for mass chat control: “There is no way to implement  such proposals related to end-to-end encrypted communication without  fundamentally undermining encryption and creating a dangerous weakness  in a core infrastructure that would have a global impact far beyond  Europe.”

The claim that content is still being “checked before” its encryption  is contrary to the end-to-end principle with which WhatsApp and signal  promote itself. Signal had once developed open source technology,  WhatsApp took it over, Mark Zuckerberg has not yet touched it. According  to Whittaker, encryption and “upload moderation” do not go together –  this is an “mathematical reality” that new words could not hide either.  The EU chat control proposal is about “mass scanning” about “the same  old monitoring with a new label” using “mass scanning”.

One thing goes without saying that if the chat services were to know  about “illegal activities” due to the surveillance of image content and  Internet addresses, they would not only have to inform the EU state or  supranational authorities immediately about it, but also “act quickly to  remove or block access to access it”. The AI-supported detection of  supposedly illegal content would therefore also result in its deletion.
Whittaker: We are previously leaving the EU market

Already in May, Whittaker announced that he would rely on the EU  market rather than engage in an undermining of encryption technology.  Now Signal has remained a niche provider with 40 million users  worldwide.

In addition to the head of the Signal, the Society for Freedom Rights also protest the organisation European Digital Rights (entitled “Be scanned – or get banned!”) and the Center for Democracy & Technology (CDT) Europe strongly against the draft regulation of the Belgian Presidency.

However, even the industry giant WhatsApp recently threatened with  its retirement from India within 60 days, according to the trade  magazines Rest of World and Inside Digital.  The government had previously adopted a regulation requiring  significant services (those with more than five million users) to  disclose the first author of information. With half a billion users in  India, WhatsApp belongs to this category, similar to what is a “very  large platform” under the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) and is  therefore subject to EU censorship law. Due to the importance of  WhatsApp for the Indian economy, a compromise is expected.

In the EU, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria and Poland  have been against the plans. Now the Belgians were apparently able to  capture France through the concession for security services and the  military. The blocking minority in the Council could therefore tip this  Wednesday. It is frightening that the conditions in the EU Council have  become so scarce that a majority is tangible. Estonia, Finland, Greece,  Italy, Portugal, Sweden, Slovenia and the Czech Republic have not yet  determined.

The European Parliament in Strasbourg-Brussels spoke out in November  to maintain chat encryption. If the Council decision is taken on  Wednesday, then perhaps the hour of this Parliament could really beat:  it would then have to do everything possible to prevent chat control in  the so-called 'trilogue' of the three EU institutions.

BASSETERRE, ST. KITTS — October 1, 2026 — Major pushback is expected at Port Zante today as scores of taxi and tour operators voice strong dissatisfaction with the St. Kitts Tourism Authority’s decision to introduce a No-Solicitation Zone in the Port Zante Courtyard.

The measure takes effect today, October 1, following a memorandum dated September 30 and addressed to all taxi and tour operators. The notice states that the Ministry of Tourism and the St. Kitts Tourism Authority will conduct a trial under which the courtyard immediately outside the cruise arrival hall becomes a No-Solicitation Zone. 

According to the SKTA, the trial is intended to improve the arrival experience for cruise visitors by reducing unsolicited approaches. Operators were asked to comply, while the Authority said the initiative would be monitored and that feedback would be encouraged. 

But several operators are objecting not only to the policy itself, but also to the way it was introduced.

Operators speaking about the development say the notice effectively gives them less than 24 hours to adjust to a significant change in how they have traditionally sought business from visitors leaving cruise ships. They argue that soliciting passengers for island tours and taxi services has long formed part of the working system at Port Zante and that such a change should have been preceded by meaningful consultation with the people whose livelihoods are directly affected.

Those concerns are claims from operators and have not been independently confirmed as the position of every taxi or tour operator. The memorandum itself does not describe any prior consultation process. It simply announces the October 1 trial, asks operators to comply and says feedback will be considered during the assessment period. 

The timing has added to the frustration.

Port Zante’s published cruise schedule shows Royal Caribbean’s Star of the Seas scheduled to visit St. Kitts today from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.  The arrival of such a major vessel makes October 1 an important working day for taxi drivers, tour operators and other tourism service providers hoping to secure business from cruise passengers.

Against that backdrop, some operators say they consider the late notice particularly troubling.

There are expectations among sections of the taxi and tour community that operators will make their objections known at Port Zante today. At the time of writing, however, there was no independently verified announcement of the exact form, scale or duration of any planned protest action.

The controversy is especially significant because cruise tourism remains an important source of income for taxi operators, tour companies, vendors and other small businesses. Tourism officials themselves have recently highlighted the wider economic reach of cruise activity across communities in St. Kitts and Nevis.

For taxi and tour operators, however, the central issue remains consultation.

Most of you want to know what all transpired in between the ‘account withheld in India’ and the final restoration of my account. 

So here’s a quick summary. Please share so that others can take the same recourse, if need be, coz the govt seems in no mood to spare any content critical of it.

On 19th March at 12:23 AM my account was withheld in India.

Very next day, I had a conversation with @SupriyaShrinate and she told me that 12 other accounts met the same fate. She did a live session and addressed media the very same day. That highlighted the issue. The wire, Quint and alt news reported the news.

I swiftly responded to MeitY on 19th March at 4:16 AM enquiring the cause that led to this removal under section 69A. ( Haven’t received any response yet )

Next I consulted with @NakulGandhi511 upon the recommendation of @iArpitSpeaks as he had earlier met with similar fate and got his account back.

Nakul sir guided me for a week and introduced me with @apar1984 who runs @internetfreedom . 

He took over my case pro bono ( for free ) and guided me accordingly. 

On 1st of April I finally filed my writ petition. The notary, wakalatnama was all new to me coz I had never been in court till this date but barring that I had to do nothing. 

Every response, every draft was given to me by @namanbasoyaa who works with Apar sir. 

I got my listing on 6th of April with the honr Judge Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav. 

He didn’t even waste 10 mins and ordered a restore provided that the posts that warranted an action against me shall stay unblocked until the committee level hearing of MeitY ( It’s not scheduled yet )

In fact I still don’t have the blocking order that necessitated such an action against me that is ultra vires of the constitution. Section 69A doesn’t permit govt to remove pre-emotive post based on speculation and that’s exactly what govt effectively did by withholding my entire account not some posts. 

Also big thanks to my followers who stood with me. Some used VPN just to stay connected. I’m indebted to all of you and IFF and Apar sir in particular. 

Taking this opportunity to urge the govt to remove ban from other accounts as well folllwing the same precedence used in mine and @DrNimoYadav ’s case.

FoS needs to be supreme. Taking down post is wrong in itself but an entire account that took years of cultivating is just brutal and uncalled for.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

Statement on restrictions faced by cartoonists Satish Acharya and Manjul on Instagram

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly condemns the restrictions faced by cartoonists @satishacharya and @MANJULtoons on Instagram. On 26th September, Manjul’s cartoon on the Election Commission was restricted in India “pursuant to a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement.” 

Satish Acharya also repeatedly faced takedowns of his posts on Instagram, and on 28th September, his account got restricted in India. The notification shared by the cartoonist stated that the platform had to “repeatedly restrict access to content posted” by him “pursuant to legal requirements.”

In March 2026, Satish also received two notifications from @X stating that @GoI_MeitY had ordered the platform to block his content. He also received a notification from X about a content takedown request from the Cyber Crime Department of the Mumbai Police. These cartoons depicted India’s stance on US-Israel bombing on Iran and the killing of its supreme leader. Another cartoon showed the arms of state actors forming a human chain around billionaire Gautam Adani with the caption “Ek hain to safe hain.”

These notifications also stated that the platform could not provide him with additional information due to legal restrictions. This lack of transparency makes it particularly difficult to challenge a blocking order. While notifications issued by X identified the authorities that ordered the takedowns, Instagram did not disclose which authorities had ordered the takedowns. In such instances, before a creator can even consider approaching a court, they may first have to determine which government authority issued the order, under what legal provision it was issued, and what specific content or reasoning formed the basis for it. Without access to this information, exercising the right to challenge the restriction becomes significantly harder. 

Even when the information is available, going to court requires time, money, and legal assistance. All of these resources may not even be available for cartoonists, independent creators, or students. For someone facing multiple takedown orders, challenging each restriction individually can become an exhausting and expensive exercise.

@scroll_in’s article on the restrictions faced by Satish Acharya stated that the cartoonist attempted to challenge Meta’s action but was unable to reach Instagram’s help centre due to its automated grievance redressal systems and the lack of access to human support. Meta’s AI Support Assistant provides ‘In-App Appeal’ as the ‘primary method for challenging a content decision.’ However, this method is not a statutory remedy, amenable to further challenge at the Grievance Appellate Committee level. The prescribed procedure of approaching the Grievance Officer through Meta’s official reporting form does not provide a method to report the takedown of content, either for violations of Meta Community Standards, Terms of Service, or takedowns through “automated systems implemented under legal requirements.”

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also observed that the Grievance Officer email address available on the website can only be used to enquire about the grievance redressal mechanism and not to file a Grievance Officer report. This also creates a structural barrier to access further remedies, such as approaching the Grievance Appellate Committee, which mandatorily requires a Grievance Officer report to be filed prior to filing an appeal.

In the past few months, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has recorded similar instances of restrictions faced by other cartoonists in India. In August 2026, @cartoonistrrs's posts showing a comical representation of the PM’s viral reel received a takedown notice, and @cartoonistvish faced 4 takedown orders for his cartoon criticising Prime Minister Narender Modi’s foreign travels during domestic issues. Even a simple satire by @BagchiAsh, showing the PM with a Melody chocolate on his forehead, was restricted on Meta.

Over time, such instances of censorship can have consequences far beyond individual takedowns. When creators repeatedly see their work removed without clear explanations and realise that the only meaningful way to challenge the decision may be through costly legal proceedings, they may begin to censor themselves. The uncertainty surrounding what can be taken down and the difficulty of fighting back when takedowns happen can eventually discourage people from creating altogether. If the cost of speaking becomes too high and the consequences too unpredictable, creators may censor themselves or give up on their art entirely.

The increasing trend of censorship of cartoons and political humour is deeply concerning, particularly because it points to a shrinking space for dissent in India. The right to freedom of speech and expression is a fundamental right, and the ability to question, criticise and even ridicule those in power is an essential part of a democratic society. Dissent may be uncomfortable for governments, but discomfort cannot be the basis for silencing it.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls upon @Meta to remove restrictions on Satish Acharya’s posts and account and Manjul’s Instagram posts with immediate effect. https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 further calls upon the Government to provide greater transparency about the legal and policy basis for content restrictions on cartoons and satirical content. The Government should also ensure that the users are provided with meaningful, accessible, and timely avenues for content takedowns and account restrictions.
